newsitem.title: USA: No U.S. decision yet on Mexico drug certification.
newsitem.headline: No U.S. decision yet on Mexico drug certification.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton has not yet decided whether to certify Mexico as an ally in the war against illegal drugs, the White House said on Saturday.

Officials disputed a New York Times report that the Clinton administration plans to certify Mexico as helping in America's anti-drug effort despite official shock over the recent arrest of the Mexican government's top anti-drug official on charges he had links to drug traffickers.

A White House spokeswoman, Mary Ellen Glynn, said a recommendation on the matter had not yet been forwarded from the U.S. State Department's bureau of international narcotics to Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who in turn will make her recommendation to Clinton.

"The White House has not received the recommendation from the State Department on drug certification of any country so its premature to prejudge the decision by the secretary of state," she said. The White House expected the recommendation by the end of the month, she added.

Clinton has to grade Mexico and 31 other countries at the end of the month in the "certification" process, Washington's annual evaluation of other governments' fight against drugs. Countries that fail that test may be subjected to U.S. economic and trade sanctions.
Clinton is to visit Mexico for talks with President Ernesto Zedillo on April 11-12.

The United States has always certified its southern neighbour and third-largest trade partner, despite evidence of high-level corruption and the fact that most drugs enter its territory through the 2,000-mile (3,200-km) U.S.-Mexican border.

But a complicating issue was the arrest on Feb. 6 of Mexico's top anti-narcotics official, Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, on charges of collaborating with a powerful narcotics trafficker. Gutierrez had been to Washington on a visit last month and reportedly received a classified briefing on U.S. anti-drug operations.
Clinton told reporters on Thursday that the case of Gutierrez would be a "mixed factor" in his decision.

Nine U.S. lawmakers urged Clinton on Saturday to ease sanctions on Colombia, which was punished last year with the cut off of most U.S. aid and support for loans from multilateral banks for failing to stem the flow of illegal drugs.
